name: Dovecot
version_context: Development snapshot at commit 7b8041031d56b40e93eb794cb0b2e507ed1e9d7d; main documentation is rolling, and 2.3 design documents are historical context corroborated against this source
summary: A security-oriented mail server that separates least-privilege protocol login from asynchronous authentication, user lookup, post-login mail processes, mailbox indexes, and pluggable storage backends.

features.name: Split login, authentication, and mail processes
features.description: Dovecot divides work among master, config, log, auth, protocol-specific login, and post-login mail processes. Login processes implement the minimum pre-authentication protocol surface, auth verifies credentials and performs userdb lookup, and mail processes handle post-login work with the logged-in user's privileges.
benefits: Separates untrusted pre-authentication code from mailbox access
Allows process-specific privilege and resource limits
Keeps authentication and protocol handling reusable across IMAP, POP3, and related services
costs: UNIX-socket handoffs and final authentication checks add lifecycle complexity
A blocked or overloaded auth master can delay many logins
Process limits and service settings become part of capacity planning

features.name: Asynchronous passdb and userdb authentication pipeline
features.description: The auth process receives requests from login clients over its authentication protocol, selects a SASL mechanism, verifies credentials through passdb or credential lookup, and returns userdb information to the mail process. Long-running lookups and password-hash verification may use auth workers, while multiple requests can proceed asynchronously.
benefits: Supports multiple authentication mechanisms and database backends
Prevents slow external lookups from blocking the auth master directly
Makes credential verification and user privilege data separate stages
costs: A successful credential check can still fail during userdb or final verification
Passdb, userdb, mechanism, and proxy settings create a large policy surface
Authentication protocol versioning and trust assumptions must remain aligned

features.name: Mailbox index and pluggable storage boundary
features.description: Dovecot exposes mailbox operations through mail-storage and mailbox abstractions, with storage backends implementing allocation, namespace attachment, mailbox allocation, purge, and related operations. IMAP state uses mail indexes and mailbox transactions so protocol-visible flags, UIDs, metadata, and message changes can be synchronized with backend storage.
benefits: Allows mailbox formats and storage backends to share protocol-facing abstractions
Indexes accelerate mailbox state and synchronization operations
Transactions provide an explicit boundary for grouped mailbox changes
costs: Index and message-body consistency must be maintained across crashes and concurrent access
Backend-specific capabilities and locking behavior remain observable
Storage plugins expand the operational and compatibility surface

features.name: Protocol-specific login isolation and session limits
features.description: Dovecot uses separate login services for protocols such as IMAP, POP3, ManageSieve, and submission. Login processes run in restricted environments, can be bounded by service process and client limits, and transfer an authenticated connection to a post-login mail process; this implementation boundary is distinct from the IMAP or POP3 protocol specifications.
benefits: Makes protocol admission and mailbox access separate trust zones
Bounds unauthenticated connection pressure and process resource use
Allows protocol-specific front ends to share auth and storage services
costs: Connection handoff and hibernation add state-transfer paths
Too-low limits reject or evict clients under load while too-high limits increase exposure
Protocol compliance does not determine storage durability or authentication policy

features.name: Least-privilege boundaries and failure separation
features.description: Dovecot's process split assigns different privileges and restricts protocol-facing code. Login services can run in a restricted chroot, auth verifies ordinary credential-based logins, and mail processes use authenticated user context. The trust boundary has exceptions: auth trusts connection metadata and client-certificate identity/trust reported by login processes, so isolation is not an unconditional guarantee against a compromised login process.
benefits: Reduces the impact of vulnerabilities in pre-authentication and TLS code
Requires independent credential verification for ordinary password-based logins
Makes operational diagnosis distinguish auth, user lookup, protocol, and storage failures
costs: Privilege transitions and socket permissions must be configured coherently
Security isolation can add IPC, process, and debugging overhead
Failure diagnosis must follow state across multiple process classes
Client-certificate authentication inherits trust in the login process's certificate verification

features.name: LMTP local delivery and recipient-specific failures
features.description: Dovecot's LMTP local-delivery path looks up the recipient's storage user, optionally checks per-user concurrency through anvil, and invokes mail_deliver for each local recipient. It reports 250 Saved on success, temporary 451 replies for internal or delivery errors, 552 for rejection, and configurable temporary or permanent quota replies. These are delivery results returned to the upstream sender, distinct from IMAP mailbox access and from a durable MTA retry queue.
benefits: Returns separate delivery outcomes for recipients sharing one transaction
Uses the mail user's storage and delivery settings at the delivery boundary
Exposes temporary failures and quota policy to the upstream queueing MTA
costs: The upstream sender must retain and retry temporary failures
Quota policy changes whether failure is retryable or permanent
A lost success reply can make a retry ambiguous; this path does not establish exactly-once delivery

mathematical_views.question: How does a connection move from protocol login through SASL exchange, passdb verification, userdb lookup, final authorization, mail-process handoff, and session teardown?
assumptions: A connection has unauthenticated, authenticating, authenticated, authorized, active, and terminated states
Passdb success and userdb success are separate transitions
Ordinary credential verification is independent of the login process; certificate identity and connection metadata are trusted exceptions
The view abstracts individual IMAP and POP3 wire commands

mathematical_views.model: Mailbox synchronization and transaction state machine
mathematical_views.question: How do mailbox indexes, UIDs, flags, metadata, transactions, commits, rollbacks, and backend storage changes produce a consistent protocol-visible mailbox state?
assumptions: A mailbox is represented by backend content plus index and synchronization state
Mailbox operations occur inside explicit transaction contexts where applicable
Commit and rollback are modeled as distinct transitions with backend-dependent failure outcomes
The model does not claim that every storage backend provides identical crash guarantees
If mailbox IDs become inconsistent, recovery can require closing and reopening the mailbox, forcing an IMAP disconnect

mathematical_views.question: How are master, login, auth, auth-worker, mail, storage, and logging processes connected, and which transitions cross a trust or privilege boundary?
assumptions: Process classes and storage resources are distinct vertex types; storage libraries execute within mail processes rather than implying a dedicated storage daemon
Login-to-auth and login-to-mail handoffs are separate authorization boundaries
Chroot, user, group, and service limits are deployment-dependent labels
The graph distinguishes Dovecot's IMAP implementation from the IMAP protocol standard

mathematical_views.question: Which recipients completed mailbox delivery, which need upstream retry, and which have permanent failure after a shared LMTP transaction?
assumptions: For recipients R, state is a vector o in {pending, saved, temporary-failure, permanent-failure}^R
User lookup and concurrency checks precede local delivery; each recipient result is determined independently by its delivery path
A 250 reply follows successful mail_deliver, while 4xx preserves the upstream sender's retry obligation
Observing no reply cannot distinguish a failed save from a successful save followed by connection loss; external deduplication is not assumed

benefits: Protocol, authentication, and mailbox privileges are independently bounded
costs: IPC handoffs and coordinated lifecycles increase complexity

benefits: Slow or parallel credential backends do not require blocking one auth request at a time
costs: Multiple lookup and final-verification stages create more failure transitions

benefits: Protocol state can share stable abstractions across mailbox formats
costs: Index, transaction, lock, and backend semantics must remain coherent

benefits: Admission pressure and pre-authentication exposure are explicitly bounded
costs: Capacity limits and handoff state can reject clients or add latency

benefits: Compromise and failure domains are narrower than a single all-privileged server process
costs: Cross-process debugging and configuration become more demanding

benefits: Mailbox delivery exposes recipient-specific success and retryable failure
costs: Upstream retries and lost acknowledgements require end-to-end failure handling
